**Section D: Essay (10 marks).** Write an essay of between 250 and 300 words on any one of the following topics. You are strongly advised to plan your work and write at least one draft before you write the final version.

**Topic 1.** You have been invited by the young people in your village to make a speech during Youth Week on the causes of crime in the village. In your speech you may want to talk about the importance of a good family life, religion, friends and so on. Write the speech without mentioning the name of your village.
questions.corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode
La rédaction anglaise du BAC sanctionne autant le respect du format imposé (discours devant un public de jeunes, article de journal argumentatif, argumentaire oral destiné à un panel) que le contenu. Un discours s'adresse directement à un auditoire avec un ton engageant ; un article de journal développe une position structurée avec des arguments clairs pour un lectorat qu'on ne connaît pas personnellement ; un argumentaire devant un panel doit anticiper et démonter les objections implicites de ses interlocuteurs plutôt que de simplement affirmer une opinion. Comme le sujet propose un choix, un seul texte doit être rédigé le jour de l'examen ; les modèles ci-dessous illustrent chacun l'un des formats possibles.

## Topic 1 - Speech (modèle, environ 270 mots)

Dear friends,

Thank you for inviting me to speak during this Youth Week on a subject that concerns all of us: why crime keeps finding its way into our community, even among people we grew up with.

I do not believe anyone is born a criminal. Most of the young people who end up committing crimes started out exactly like the rest of us, but somewhere along the way, something important was missing. Very often, that missing piece is a stable family life. A young person who grows up without guidance, without someone checking where they spend their evenings or who they spend them with, is far more likely to drift towards bad company than one who feels genuinely watched over and cared for at home.

Religion, whatever form it takes for each of us, also plays its part. It is not simply about attending a place of worship; it is about the values it teaches, honesty, respect for others, patience, which do not disappear the moment we leave the building. Young people who hold onto these values, even loosely, tend to think twice before harming someone else for personal gain.

Friends matter just as much. We become, more than we like to admit, like the people we spend the most time with. A young person surrounded by friends who see stealing or violence as normal will slowly start to see it as normal too, while one surrounded by friends who value hard work and honesty will lean in that same direction instead.

None of us can fix every family, every friendship or every personal struggle by ourselves. But we can choose, starting today, to be the kind of friend, the kind of family member, that quietly makes crime a little less likely for someone close to us.

Thank you.

**Topic 2.** Imagine that in your local newspaper, Youth and Tomorrow, there have been many articles lately of judges inflicting severe prison sentences on young offenders for minor crimes. Write an article, which you may have published in the local paper, giving your reasons why young people should not be given severe prison sentences for minor crimes. You do not need to write your address in the article. Your name should be Marcel Nang.
questions.corrige_markdown:
## Topic 2 - Newspaper article (modèle, environ 260 mots)

**Severe Prison Sentences Are Not the Answer for Young Offenders**

By Marcel Nang

Recent articles in this newspaper have described judges handing down severe prison sentences to young people for relatively minor crimes. I understand the desire to appear tough on crime, but I believe this approach does far more harm than good.

First, prison exposes young offenders, often first-time ones, to hardened criminals who can teach them far worse habits than the minor offence that put them there in the first place. A teenager sent to prison for a small theft may leave months later having learned how to commit much more serious crimes, surrounded by people for whom crime is a way of life.

Second, a prison sentence permanently marks a young person's record, closing doors to education and employment long after the original offence is forgotten by everyone except the justice system. This often pushes young people back towards crime simply because legitimate opportunities have been taken away from them by the very punishment meant to correct their behaviour.

Third, alternatives such as community service, mandatory counselling, or supervised restitution to victims address the harm caused without cutting the young offender off from school, family and the ordinary structures that could still guide them towards a better path.

None of this means minor crimes should go unpunished. But a punishment should aim to correct behaviour, not manufacture a more determined criminal by the time a young person is released. I urge our judges to reserve severe prison sentences for serious crimes, and to consider more constructive alternatives for the minor ones.

**Section D: Essay (10 marks).** Write an essay of between 250 and 300 words on any one of the following topics. You are strongly advised to plan your work and write at least one draft before you write the final version.

**Topic 3.** Imagine that you have been selected to be on a panel choosing a leader of the young people in your village. During the interviews on the first day, you noticed that the girls were not given a fair opportunity. Write an argument that may be presented to the other members of the panel to convince them that a girl could be a good group leader.
questions.corrige_markdown:
## Topic 3 - Argument for a panel (modèle, environ 250 mots)

Fellow panel members,

Before we continue the interviews tomorrow, I want to raise a concern I noticed today: the girls who came before us were asked fewer questions, and often less serious ones, than the boys, as though we had already decided, without saying so, that a girl could not really lead this group.

I do not think any of us intended this, but I believe we should correct it, because nothing in what we saw today actually supports treating the candidates differently. Several of the girls we interviewed spoke with real clarity about the group's problems and proposed solutions at least as detailed as those given by the boys, yet we spent noticeably less time testing their ideas.

Leadership does not depend on gender; it depends on judgement, the ability to listen, and the willingness to take responsibility when things go wrong, qualities we have seen in candidates of both sexes today. If we allow an unspoken assumption to quietly decide this outcome before we have even finished the interviews, we risk choosing a weaker leader for our young people simply because we did not give every candidate an equal chance to prove themselves.

I am not asking that we favour any girl for the sake of it. I am asking that tomorrow, we ask every remaining candidate, girl or boy, the same searching questions we would ask anyone we were seriously considering for this responsibility, and let their answers, not our assumptions, decide who leads.
